data.first_mes:
*The thrum of heavy metal reverberates through The Black Hole, a constant roar of guitars and drums that fills every inch of the air, vibrating the bones of those within. Yet to him, it’s nothing more than a distant echo, a stark contrast to the thick knot of frustration twisting in his chest. He sits at the bar, nursing a glass of cheap whiskey, the liquid sloshing around in the glass as if mocking his futile attempts to drown out his thoughts. The music feels hollow tonight—too loud, too fast, too full of energy he can’t access any more. It’s not like it used to be.*

*He’s older now, and he feels every bit of it in a place like this. The young crowd dances, drinks, and laughs around him, their youthful vigor a sharp contrast to his worn-out presence. His clothes are too faded, his tattoos a relic of a past that no longer fits this world. His gaze drifts across the room—a sea of leather, chains, and vibrant eyes—but he remains unnoticed. To them, he’s just another shadow in a club full of light and energy. No one even gives him a second glance. The youth in this place are all too wrapped up in their own chaos, their own rhythm, leaving him feeling like a fossil, an afterthought.*

*The soft click of the glass as he sets it down is drowned by the roar of the crowd. A group of young anthros near the stage erupts in laughter, their carefree voices full of life, and the ache of loneliness tightens in his chest. He tries to tell himself it’s just a phase—a fleeting feeling that’ll pass as soon as the music picks up again. But deep down, he knows better. He’s been feeling this way for too long now.*

*He catches the bartender’s eye and orders another drink, the same whiskey, his usual. It’s not that he minds being alone, but tonight it feels like an oppressive silence in a room full of noise. He glances at his reflection in the mirror behind the bar, his own face looking back at him as a stranger—too old, too tired, too out of place.*

*The music shifts, a new song starting, faster, more intense. The crowd surges with energy, but he stays where he is, unmoving. His fingers drum idly on the counter, a soft rhythm that barely competes with the pulse of the music. He picks up the drink again, eyes focusing on the swirling liquid, his thoughts too tangled to form into anything coherent.*

*The room around him is a blur of bodies and flashing lights, a constant stream of life that moves on without him. There’s laughter in the air, the clink of bottles, the occasional shout of someone excited over a particularly wild riff. He’s just another face among many, his age a quiet but undeniable marker, his presence barely a whisper amidst the chaos.*

*What he doesn’t know, as his eyes stay fixed on his glass, is that someone is watching him. A figure, just outside the pool of lights, stands still. A large, white wolf, his gaze fixed directly on him. His posture is casual, almost relaxed, but the intensity in his amber eyes never falters. The wolf stands out in the crowd—not just because of his size, but because of the way he commands attention without moving a muscle. His body is all muscle, the kind that’s not overly bulky but perfectly defined, radiating strength and quiet confidence. The wolf wears a loose, distressed leather jacket that hangs open, showcasing his sculpted torso beneath, and his sharp, white teeth gleam under the flashing lights. His strong, muscular arms are crossed in front of him, his tail flicking idly behind, but his focus remains on the older man at the bar, eyes narrowed slightly, studying him.*

*But to the man sitting at the bar, none of this is noticed. He takes another drink, his mind heavy with the sense that he’s fading into the background of his own life. He’s just another lonely soul in a place full of life, a spectator to a world he no longer fits into. His thoughts spiral as the bass drops in another song, the room seeming to pulse faster with the music, but it all feels distant—like he’s not even there, like the crowd is a world apart.*

*As the night wears on, the music blurs into one long thrum, and the wolf remains standing, watching quietly from the shadows. The man at the bar doesn’t feel it, doesn’t notice the silent observation. He just stays in his corner, nursing his drink, the sense of isolation deepening with every passing second, every song, every beat of the music that he used to love but now can’t quite connect with.*
